It very much varies between schools. The professor I had at [University A] for 1 and 2 is good friends with the professor for the same at [University B], and apparently they did things very differently than we do.

In theory 1 our final was to write two 4 bar counterpoint exercises following T, PD, D form. 

In theory 2 we covered diatonic harmony, applied dominants of different flavors, small forms, sequences, and modulations. The composition part of the final was to write a 24-32 bar string quartet in ABA’ form that modulates, has allied dominants and sequences. This was played for the class. 

Tbh theory wasn’t bad, I hated Aural training (at least that’s our name for the class) way more. Singing was a pita. 

I managed to find the old syllabus for theory 2 on my computer, and files for my finals on my notation software.

Definitely technique. If you can, I’d highly suggest getting a well-known musician’s 50 lessons for xylophone. It will not only help with technique but really work on a lot of fundamentals and help you with more difficult passages as you keep playing. 

I’ve actually been going back through the first few lessons while practicing this past week or so. I normally spend around 4-5 hours easily on the exercises for each lesson. 

Also, just keep playing, even if your only practice is 5 minute stretches a couple times a day walking up to the board and playing a piece you know. It will really help with being prepared for performances and general confidence with a piece. It’s one of the methods I used to prepare for a masterclass I played in recently.

The biggest thing about other sports is the fact that it’s give and take between athletes and officials. One sport sees both groups throwing “fuck you”’s to one another, another has some friendly banter. Another sport is the outlier. One thing can get you tossed from the game and the ump has complete impunity and control over a game. There are so many awful calls that can each change the outcome of the game in specific situations; especially those with historically bad zone calling.

That’s how I feel. Screw having a traditional closer when you’ve got a high tension situation and you need some strikeouts but raisel in to get you where you need to be, whether it’s in the 7, 8 or 9th inning.

National doctrine for most of the conflict dictated that the primary objective of the main battle tank was not to engage armored vehicles directly, but to support the infantry and perform other roles where the 75mm gun and its superior high-explosive capability were preferred, such as against soft targets. It was primarily the tank destroyer branch tasked with responding to breakthroughs by enemy armored vehicles, utilizing platforms characterized by high speed, light armor, and more powerful anti-tank guns. The Americans desired turreted tank destroyers, leading them to employ smaller-caliber guns firing high-velocity rounds, such as the 3-inch gun used in the early stages of the war. The tank destroyer branch typically operated closer to supply lines, making it more feasible to manage a variety of shell calibers, whereas maintaining such diversity for frontline tank units was more challenging. The fact that support vehicles for the Sherman had larger and more potent guns is largely a matter of doctrinal difference rather than technical limitation. The interwar period was focused on developing combat tactics for a rapidly evolving form of warfare, similar to the development of aerial combat tactics.
